stimuli.title: Masters of Disguise
stimuli.text:
An octopus resting on a reef can vanish in less than a second. One moment a diver sees a reddish animal clinging to a rock; the next, there is only rock, speckled and bumpy, exactly like everything around it. Few animals can change their appearance as quickly or as completely.

The trick lies in the skin. Just beneath the surface sit thousands of tiny sacs called chromatophores, each filled with a pigment such as yellow, red, brown or black. Every sac is ringed by small muscles. When the muscles pull, the sac stretches wide and its color spreads like a drop of ink; when they relax, the sac shrinks to a dot that is almost invisible. Because nerves from the brain control these muscles, an octopus can change color in a fraction of a second.

Color is only part of the disguise. An octopus can also raise small bumps on its skin, called papillae, to copy the rough texture of coral or seaweed. Some even change their posture, curling their arms to look like a clump of algae.

Strangely, scientists believe that most octopuses cannot see color the way people do. Their eyes have only one type of light-detecting cell. How, then, do they match their surroundings so well? Researchers are still investigating. One idea is that octopuses judge brightness and pattern rather than color; another is that their skin itself may sense light. For now, the octopus remains one of the ocean's most puzzling performers.

stimuli.title: The Keeper of Lime Rock
stimuli.text:
In the 1800s, a lighthouse did not run itself. Someone had to climb the tower each evening, trim the wick, polish the glass and keep the lamp burning until dawn. On a tiny island of rock in the harbor of Newport, Rhode Island, that someone was often a teenager named Ida Lewis.

Ida's father was the keeper of the Lime Rock lighthouse, but soon after the family moved there he became seriously ill. Ida took over much of the work. Because the rock had no bridge to shore, she also rowed her younger brothers and sister to school each day, and she became one of the strongest rowers in the harbor.

That skill mattered. In 1869, two soldiers crossing the harbor were thrown into the water when their boat overturned in rough weather. Ida, who reportedly rushed out without stopping for a coat or shoes, rowed out and pulled them into her boat. News of the rescue spread to newspapers across the country, and visitors began arriving just to meet the young woman who had braved the icy water.

Ida did not enjoy the fuss. She said she was only doing her job, and she kept doing it for decades. In 1879 she was officially appointed keeper, and over the years she was credited with saving many people from the harbor. Long after her death, the lighthouse was renamed in her honor.

stimuli.title: The Wall on Ferris Street
stimuli.text:
For as long as Dev could remember, the side of the laundromat on Ferris Street had been a blank gray wall, the kind of wall nobody noticed until someone sprayed a scribble on it and someone else painted over the scribble with a slightly different gray.

So when a sign appeared announcing a Neighborhood Mural Day, Dev rolled his eyes. "Nobody's going to show up," he told his grandmother. She handed him an old shirt anyway. "Then you'll have plenty of room to paint," she said.

More than forty people showed up. An artist named Ms. Okafor had sketched the design in chalk: a river winding across the wall, with a bridge, a market and dozens of small windows waiting to be filled. Each volunteer got a window. Dev stood in front of his for a long time, brush dripping, before he painted what he knew best: his grandmother's kitchen table, with a bowl of oranges in the middle.

By evening the river was blue, the market bustled with painted shoppers, and the windows glowed with other people's tables, pets, gardens and instruments. A man Dev had never spoken to pointed at the oranges. "My mother kept fruit like that," he said.

Dev walked home slowly. He had passed that wall a thousand times, he realized, without once thinking that it belonged to him.

stimuli.title: Why Leaves Change Color
stimuli.text:
Every autumn, forests in many parts of the world put on a show of yellow, orange and red. It is tempting to think the trees are painting their leaves, but much of the color was there all summer, hidden.

A green leaf is green because of chlorophyll, the pigment that captures sunlight and lets the tree make food from water and carbon dioxide. Chlorophyll breaks down in sunlight, so all summer long the leaf keeps making more of it. The leaf also contains yellow and orange pigments called carotenoids, the same kind of pigments that color carrots and corn. In summer there is so much chlorophyll that its green hides them.

As the days grow shorter and cooler, many trees stop making chlorophyll and begin preparing to drop their leaves. The green fades, and the yellows and oranges that were there all along show through.

Reds and purples are different. They come from pigments called anthocyanins, which many trees, such as some maples, actually produce in the fall. Scientists have found that sunny days followed by cool nights tend to produce the brightest reds. That is why the same forest can look dull one autumn and blaze with color the next.

stimuli.title: Ten Days to California
stimuli.text:
In 1860, a letter from the East Coast could take weeks to reach California by ship or stagecoach. For people with urgent news, that was far too slow. In April of that year, a company launched a bold experiment: carrying mail across the West on horseback, as fast as horses could run.

The Pony Express route stretched nearly 2,000 miles, from St. Joseph, Missouri, to Sacramento, California. Along it stood a chain of stations, roughly 10 to 15 miles apart. A rider galloped from one station to the next, leaped onto a fresh horse and kept going, handing the mail pouch to a new rider after many miles. Day and night, through deserts and mountain passes, the mail kept moving. In good conditions, a letter could cross the route in about ten days.

The riders were young and light, because every extra pound slowed a horse. The work was exhausting and dangerous, and storms, rough country and accidents were constant threats.

Yet the Pony Express lasted only about a year and a half. In October 1861, workers finished a telegraph line across the country. A message that had taken ten days by horse could now travel in minutes over a wire. Within days, the Pony Express shut down. It had lost its race not to another horse but to an invention.

stimuli.title: The Loudest Room in the Library
stimuli.text:
When our town library announced that it would turn its old storage room into a makerspace, some people were upset. A library, they argued, should be a quiet place for books, not a workshop full of sewing machines, 3D printers and soldering irons.

I understand the worry, but I think it misses what libraries have always been for. Libraries exist to give everyone access to tools for learning. For most of history, the most important of those tools was the book, because books were expensive and most families could not own many. Today, a 3D printer is expensive in the same way, and a library that lends one is doing exactly what it has always done.

I have seen the change myself. On Saturday afternoons the makerspace is crowded with kids designing phone stands, retired engineers teaching wiring, and a woman who repairs her neighbors' broken lamps for free. Many of them also leave with a book under their arm: a guide to robotics, a history of flight, a novel recommended by someone at the next table.

The makerspace is noisy, it is true. But the reading room is still quiet, the shelves are still full, and the library is busier than it has been in years. A library is not a building for books. It is a building for curiosity.

stimuli.title: The Waggle Dance
stimuli.text:
A honeybee that finds a patch of flowers rich in nectar faces a problem: how can she tell thousands of her sisters where to go, when bees cannot speak and the hive is dark inside?

Her answer is a dance. Back in the hive, on the upright surface of the honeycomb, she runs a short straight line while shaking her body from side to side, then loops around and repeats it, again and again. Other bees crowd close, following her movements with their antennae.

In the mid-1900s, the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch worked out what the dance means. The direction of the straight waggle run points the way. If the bee waggles straight up the comb, the food lies in the direction of the sun; if she waggles at an angle to the right of straight up, the food lies at that same angle to the right of the sun. The length of the waggle run tells distance: the longer it lasts, the farther away the flowers are.

Not every scientist believed von Frisch at first. It seemed impossible that an insect could use a kind of symbolic map. But careful experiments supported his ideas, and in 1973 he shared a Nobel Prize for his work on animal behavior. Today the waggle dance is one of the best-studied examples of communication in the animal world.

stimuli.title: Twenty-Four Frames
stimuli.text:
Watch a stop-motion film and you might think the clay figures are alive. A rabbit twitches its nose, a sailor's coat flaps in the wind, and a crowd turns to stare. Yet none of it ever moved on its own. Every motion was built, one tiny step at a time, by human hands.

Stop-motion works because of how film is shown. A movie is a series of still pictures, called frames, usually shown at twenty-four frames per second. When the pictures flash by that quickly, the eye and brain blend them into smooth motion. A stop-motion animator takes advantage of this. She poses a puppet, takes one photograph, nudges an arm or an eyebrow a fraction of an inch, takes another, and repeats.

The work is painfully slow. Many animators save time by holding each pose for two frames, which means twelve new poses for every second of film. Even so, a skilled animator may finish only a few seconds of film in a full day. Puppets often have metal skeletons, called armatures, inside them so that they hold each pose without sagging under the hot studio lights.

Why would anyone choose such a slow art? Many animators say the answer is in the small imperfections: a thumbprint in the clay, a hair of fur that shifts between frames. Those flaws remind the audience that real hands made the world on screen, and that is part of the magic.

stimuli.title: Clinton's Ditch
stimuli.text:
In 1817, New York began digging a canal that many people thought was a foolish dream. It would run about 363 miles, from Albany on the Hudson River west to Buffalo on Lake Erie, through forests, swamps and hills. Critics mocked it as "Clinton's Ditch," after DeWitt Clinton, the governor who championed it.

Building it was enormous work. Crews cleared trees and dug through earth and rock, largely by hand and with animal power. They also built dozens of locks, water-filled chambers that raised and lowered boats where the land climbed or fell. Engineers learned as they went, since few people in the young nation had built anything like it.

When the canal opened in 1825, the critics fell silent. Boats pulled by mules and horses walking on towpaths beside the water could carry goods between the Great Lakes and New York City far more cheaply than wagons on rough roads. The cost of shipping fell sharply. Farmers in the West could sell their crops in Eastern cities, and Eastern workshops could send tools and cloth back.

Towns sprang up along the route, and New York City grew into the busiest port in the country. The "ditch" that people had laughed at had changed the shape of the nation's trade.

stimuli.title: First Shift
stimuli.text:
Tamsin had pictured her first afternoon at the animal shelter many times: puppies tumbling over her shoes, kittens purring in her lap. Instead, the volunteer coordinator handed her a bucket and a scrub brush.

"Kennels first," said Mr. Reyes. "Then, if there's time, you can sit with Biscuit."

Biscuit turned out to be a thin brown dog who stayed pressed against the back of his kennel, watching her with wide, worried eyes. When Tamsin crouched and reached toward him, he flinched.

"He came in last week," Mr. Reyes said quietly. "He doesn't trust people yet. Don't reach for him. Just be there."

So Tamsin sat on the floor outside the open kennel door and read her library book aloud, not looking at the dog. For twenty minutes nothing happened. Then she felt something warm against her knee. Biscuit had crept out and rested his chin there, so lightly it was almost like a question.

Tamsin kept reading. She did not want to scare off the answer.

questions.stem: ABUNDANT:
questions.explanation: Abundant means there is more than enough, so plentiful is closest. Scarce is its opposite.

questions.stem: FRAGILE:
questions.explanation: Something fragile breaks easily, like something delicate. Sturdy means the opposite, and an object can be valuable without being fragile.

questions.stem: TEDIOUS:
questions.explanation: A tedious task is long and dull, so boring is closest. Exciting is the opposite.

questions.stem: CANDID:
questions.explanation: A candid answer is open and honest. Candid sounds like candy, but it has nothing to do with sweet.

questions.stem: RELUCTANT:
questions.explanation: A reluctant helper does not want to help, so unwilling is closest. Eager is the opposite.

questions.stem: VIGILANT:
questions.explanation: A vigilant guard stays alert and watchful. Vigilant and violent look alike but are unrelated.

questions.stem: FRUGAL:
questions.explanation: A frugal person spends carefully and avoids waste, which is what thrifty means. Wasteful is the opposite, and fruitful only looks similar.

questions.stem: INTREPID:
questions.explanation: An intrepid explorer is bold and fearless. Timid, meaning shy and easily frightened, is the opposite.

questions.stem: AMBIGUOUS:
questions.explanation: An ambiguous statement can be read more than one way, so its meaning is unclear. Obvious is the opposite, and ambitious only sounds similar.

questions.stem: ELATED:
questions.explanation: Elated means extremely happy, so joyful is closest. Gloomy is the opposite.

questions.stem:
Because the old bridge was _____, the town closed it until repairs were finished.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: The clue is that the town closed the bridge for repairs, which happens when a bridge is unsafe. A famous or scenic bridge would have no reason to close.

questions.stem:
The recipe was so _____ that even a beginner could follow it.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: Even a beginner could follow it, so the recipe must be simple. Complex is the opposite of what the clue describes.

questions.stem:
Jaden was _____ to share his science project, so he volunteered to present first.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: Volunteering to go first shows that he wanted to share, so eager fits. Afraid and reluctant would make him wait, not volunteer.

questions.stem:
Mara is usually talkative, but at the meeting she was oddly _____.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: The word but signals a contrast with talkative, so the answer must mean the opposite: quiet. Chatty means the same as talkative.

questions.stem:
Although the hallway was crowded, the principal's voice was _____ enough to be heard by everyone.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: To be heard by everyone in a crowded hall, the voice had to be loud. Soft and faint would make it harder to hear.

questions.stem:
The drought made water so _____ that families were asked to water their gardens less often.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: A drought means little rain, so water was limited and people had to save it. Plentiful is the opposite of what a drought causes.

questions.stem:
Scientists remain _____ about the theory because no experiment has yet confirmed it.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: With no experiment to confirm it, scientists cannot be sure, so they are doubtful. Certain is the opposite.

questions.stem:
The coach praised the team's _____: they kept trying even when they were far behind.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: Keeping on trying when far behind is persistence, which the colon then explains. Talent and luck are not described by the second half of the sentence.

questions.stem:
The museum guide's explanation was _____: in just two sentences she covered the whole history of the vase.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: Covering a whole history in two sentences is the definition of concise. Lengthy is the opposite.

questions.stem:
The detective found the story _____, since the suspect's account changed every time he told it.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: A story that keeps changing makes a detective suspect it is untrue, so suspicious fits. A changing story is not convincing or accurate.

questions.stem: A number is divisible by both 4 and 6. Which number could it be?
questions.explanation: 36 ÷ 4 = 9 and 36 ÷ 6 = 6. Each other number fails one test: 18 and 30 are not divisible by 4, and 20 is not divisible by 6.

questions.stem: Which is the best estimate of 49 × 21?
questions.explanation: 49 is close to 50 and 21 is close to 20, and 50 × 20 = 1,000. The exact product, 1,029, is very close.

questions.stem: The ratio of red marbles to blue marbles in a bag is 2 to 3. There are 12 red marbles. How many blue marbles are there?
questions.explanation: 12 red is 6 groups of 2, so there are 6 groups of 3 blue: 18. The number 30 is the total of both colors.

questions.stem: If n is an odd number, which expression must be even?
questions.explanation: One more than an odd number is always even. Adding 2 to an odd number keeps it odd, 2n + 1 is always odd, and 3 times an odd number is odd.

questions.stem: A spinner has 8 equal sections: 3 red, 4 blue and 1 green. What is the probability of landing on blue?
questions.explanation: 4 of the 8 equal sections are blue, and 4/8 = 1/2. The fraction 3/8 is the probability of red.

questions.stem: A rectangle has a perimeter of 20 cm and a length of 6 cm. What is its width?
questions.explanation: Half the perimeter, 10 cm, is one length plus one width, so the width is 10 - 6 = 4 cm. Subtracting 6 from 20 forgets that there are two lengths and two widths.

questions.stem: The mean of four numbers is 10. What is the sum of the four numbers?
questions.explanation: The mean is the sum divided by how many numbers there are, so the sum is 10 × 4 = 40.

questions.stem: A pattern begins 3, 7, 11, 15, and continues by adding the same number each time. What is the 10th term?
questions.explanation: Each term adds 4, and the 10th term has had 9 additions: 3 + 9 × 4 = 39. Using 10 additions gives 43.

questions.stem: Which fraction is between 1/3 and 1/2?
questions.explanation: 1/3 is about 0.33 and 1/2 is 0.5, and 2/5 = 0.4 lies between them. 1/4 is too small, and 3/5 and 2/3 are greater than 1/2.

questions.stem: A train leaves at 10:45 a.m. and the trip takes 2 hours and 30 minutes. When does it arrive?
questions.explanation: Two hours after 10:45 a.m. is 12:45 p.m., and 30 minutes more is 1:15 p.m.

questions.stem:
**Column A:** 3/4

**Column B:** 0.7

Which statement is true?
options: The quantity in Column A is greater.
The quantity in Column B is greater.
The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: 3/4 = 0.75, which is greater than 0.7, so the quantity in Column A is greater.

questions.stem:
**Column A:** 25% of 80

**Column B:** 80% of 25

Which statement is true?
options: The quantity in Column A is greater.
The quantity in Column B is greater.
The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: 25% of 80 is 20, and 80% of 25 is also 20. Swapping the percent and the number gives the same product.

questions.stem:
**Column A:** The number of days in 3 weeks

**Column B:** The number of hours in 1 day

Which statement is true?
options: The quantity in Column A is greater.
The quantity in Column B is greater.
The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: 3 weeks have 21 days and a day has 24 hours, so Column B is greater.

questions.stem:
**Column A:** The perimeter of a square with sides 5 inches long

**Column B:** The perimeter of a rectangle 4 inches by 6 inches

Which statement is true?
options: The quantity in Column A is greater.
The quantity in Column B is greater.
The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: The square's perimeter is 4 × 5 = 20 inches and the rectangle's is 2 × (4 + 6) = 20 inches, so they are equal.

questions.stem:
**Column A:** 2³

**Column B:** 3²

Which statement is true?
options: The quantity in Column A is greater.
The quantity in Column B is greater.
The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: 2³ = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 and 3² = 3 × 3 = 9, so Column B is greater.

questions.stem:
**Column A:** The area of a triangle with a base of 8 cm and a height of 6 cm

**Column B:** The area of a rectangle 4 cm by 5 cm

Which statement is true?
options: The quantity in Column A is greater.
The quantity in Column B is greater.
The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: The triangle's area is half of 8 × 6, which is 24 square cm; the rectangle's is 20 square cm.

questions.stem:
**Column A:** The mean of 2, 4, 6 and 8

**Column B:** The median of 1, 5 and 9

Which statement is true?
options: The quantity in Column A is greater.
The quantity in Column B is greater.
The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: The mean is 20 ÷ 4 = 5 and the median, the middle value, is 5, so they are equal.

questions.stem:
x is a whole number.

**Column A:** x²

**Column B:** x

Which statement is true?
options: The quantity in Column A is greater.
The quantity in Column B is greater.
The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: If x = 0 or x = 1 the two are equal, but if x = 2 then x² = 4 is greater. Different values of x give different results, so the relationship cannot be determined.

questions.stem:
a and b are positive whole numbers, and a + b = 10.

**Column A:** a

**Column B:** b

Which statement is true?
options: The quantity in Column A is greater.
The quantity in Column B is greater.
The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: a could be 7 and b 3, or a could be 2 and b 8. Knowing only the sum does not tell you which is larger.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Octopuses use their skin to hide with great speed.
Octopuses are the most colorful animals in the sea.
Divers often lose sight of animals on coral reefs.
Scientists have shown that octopuses see in color.
questions.explanation: Every paragraph is about how octopuses disguise themselves through their skin. The passage says most octopuses probably cannot see color, so that option contradicts it.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what makes a chromatophore spread its color?
options: Muscles that pull the sac wide
Ink released into the nearby water
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says that when the muscles around each sac pull, the sac stretches wide and its color spreads. Ink is only a comparison.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that an octopus changes its appearance mainly to:
questions.explanation: Words like vanish and disguise, and the octopus matching the rock and coral around it, point to hiding. Nothing in the passage mentions warmth, signals or hunger.

questions.stem: As used in the second paragraph, the word "ringed" most nearly means:
questions.explanation: Each sac is ringed by small muscles, meaning the muscles form a ring around it. Sounded is the meaning of ringing a bell, which does not fit here.

questions.stem: How is the passage organized?
options: It tells one diver's story from start to finish.
It compares the octopus with many other sea animals.
It describes a skill, explains it, then raises a question.
It argues that coral reefs need more protection.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph shows the disguise, the middle paragraphs explain how skin color and texture work, and the last asks how a colorblind animal matches colors. The diver appears only briefly.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the octopus is best described as:
questions.explanation: The author calls the octopus one of the ocean's most puzzling performers and describes its tricks with wonder. Nothing suggests fear or doubt.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why Newport built a new harbor
A soldier's long trip across the state
A young keeper known for her courage
questions.explanation: The passage follows Ida Lewis from running the lighthouse as a teenager to her famous rescue and long career.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why did Ida row to shore every day?
options: To buy oil for the lamp
To take her siblings to school
To visit her father at the hospital
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the rock had no bridge, so she rowed her younger brothers and sister to school each day.

questions.stem: Ida's statement that she was "only doing her job" suggests that she:
options: saw her rescues as ordinary duty
wanted more pay for her work
questions.explanation: She disliked the fuss and kept working for decades, so she seems to have thought of rescues as part of the job, not as something heroic.

questions.stem: As used in the third paragraph, the word "braved" most nearly means:
questions.explanation: To brave icy water is to face it in spite of the danger. Avoided means the opposite.

questions.stem: Why does the author begin by describing a lighthouse keeper's nightly tasks?
options: To explain how lamps were first made
To show how demanding the job was
To compare old and new lighthouses
questions.explanation: Listing the climbing, trimming and polishing shows how much work a keeper did, which makes a teenager doing it more impressive.

questions.stem: Which word best describes how the author presents Ida Lewis?
questions.explanation: The author praises her skill, courage and modesty, and ends with the lighthouse renamed in her honor.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the theme of the story?
options: Artists should always plan their work alone.
Old buildings ought to be torn down.
Shared work can make a place feel like home.
Gray walls are hard to keep clean in cities.
questions.explanation: By painting the wall with his neighbors, Dev comes to feel that the wall belongs to him. The story shows an artist planning with many volunteers, not alone.

questions.stem: What did Dev paint in his window?
options: A bridge over the winding blue river
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says he painted his grandmother's kitchen table with a bowl of oranges. The bridge and market were part of Ms. Okafor's design.

questions.stem: Dev's remark that "nobody's going to show up" suggests that at first he:
options: planned to paint the whole wall alone
questions.explanation: He rolled his eyes and predicted no one would come, which shows he did not expect the neighborhood to be interested.

questions.stem: As used in the fourth paragraph, the word "bustled" most nearly means:
questions.explanation: A market that bustled with shoppers is busy and lively. Quiet and empty is the opposite.

questions.stem: How does the final paragraph relate to the rest of the story?
options: It shows how Dev's view has changed.
It explains how the mural was designed.
It brings in a new problem for Dev.
It describes the wall before the event.
questions.explanation: At the start Dev ignored the wall; at the end he realizes it belongs to him, which shows the change the day made.

questions.stem: The mood at the end of the story is best described as:
questions.explanation: Dev walks home slowly, thinking about a wall that now feels like his, after a stranger shares a memory. Nothing at the end is tense or bitter.

questions.stem: What is the greatest common factor of 36 and 48?
questions.explanation: 36 = 12 × 3 and 48 = 12 × 4, and 3 and 4 share no factor, so 12 is the greatest. 3, 4 and 6 are common factors too, but smaller.

questions.stem: If 3x + 5 = 20, what is the value of x?
questions.explanation: Subtract 5 from both sides to get 3x = 15, then divide by 3: x = 5. Stopping at 15 forgets to divide.

questions.stem: Two angles are supplementary. One measures 65°. What is the measure of the other?
questions.explanation: Supplementary angles add to 180°, and 180 - 65 = 115. 25° would make them complementary, adding to 90°.

questions.stem: What is the mode of 3, 7, 7, 8 and 10?
questions.explanation: The mode is the value that appears most often, and 7 appears twice. 35 is the sum.

questions.stem: What is -8 - (-3)?
questions.explanation: Subtracting a negative is the same as adding: -8 + 3 = -5. Getting -11 adds the 3 in the wrong direction.

questions.stem: A gym charges a \$20 sign-up fee plus \$15 a month. Which expression gives the total cost for m months?
questions.explanation: The \$20 is paid once and the \$15 is paid every month, so the cost is 20 + 15m. Writing 35m charges the sign-up fee every month.

questions.stem: How many centimeters are in 3.2 meters?
questions.explanation: There are 100 centimeters in a meter, so 3.2 × 100 = 320. Multiplying by 1,000 confuses centimeters with millimeters.

questions.stem: What is the mean of 12, 15, 18 and 15?
questions.explanation: The sum is 60 and there are 4 numbers, so the mean is 60 ÷ 4 = 15. 18 is the greatest value, not the mean.

questions.stem: What is 3/4 + 2/3?
questions.explanation: With a common denominator of 12, 9/12 + 8/12 = 17/12 = 1 5/12. Adding tops and bottoms to get 5/7 is the classic mistake.

questions.stem: What is the value of 2a² - b when a = 3 and b = 4?
questions.explanation: Square first: a² = 9, then 2 × 9 = 18 and 18 - 4 = 14. Squaring 2a instead gives 36 - 4 = 32.

questions.stem: A rectangular prism is 4 cm long, 3 cm wide and 2 cm high. What is its volume?
questions.explanation: Volume is length × width × height: 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 cubic centimeters. 52 is the surface area, and 9 adds the edges.

questions.stem: What is the range of 14, 9, 22, 17 and 11?
questions.explanation: The range is the greatest value minus the least: 22 - 9 = 13. 14.6 is the mean.

questions.stem: Which fraction is equal to 0.375?
questions.explanation: 0.375 = 375/1000, and dividing top and bottom by 125 gives 3/8. As a check, 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375.

questions.stem: Which expression is equivalent to 4(2x - 3) + x?
questions.explanation: 4(2x - 3) = 8x - 12, and adding x gives 9x - 12. Writing 9x - 3 forgets to multiply the 3 by 4.

questions.stem: On a scale drawing, 1 cm stands for 4 m. A room is 5 cm long on the drawing. How long is the real room?
questions.explanation: Each centimeter is 4 meters, so 5 cm is 5 × 4 = 20 m. Adding 5 and 4 gives 9, which is not how a scale works.

questions.stem: In a class vote, 12 students chose apples, 8 chose bananas, 10 chose grapes and 10 chose pears. What percent chose apples?
questions.explanation: 40 students voted in all, and 12 out of 40 is 0.3, or 30%. 12% treats the 12 votes as if the total were 100.

questions.stem: A shirt costs \$24 and is on sale for 25% off. What is the sale price?
questions.explanation: 25% of \$24 is \$6, and \$24 - \$6 = \$18. \$6 is the discount, not the price.

questions.stem: Which inequality shows the solution of 2x - 7 > 5?
questions.explanation: Add 7 to both sides to get 2x > 12, then divide by 2: x > 6. The sign does not flip because the 2 is positive.

questions.stem: A square and an equilateral triangle have the same perimeter. Each side of the square is 6 inches. How long is each side of the triangle?
questions.explanation: The square's perimeter is 4 × 6 = 24 inches, and the triangle's three equal sides share it: 24 ÷ 3 = 8 inches.

questions.stem: Two fair number cubes, each numbered 1 to 6, are rolled. What is the probability that the sum is 7?
questions.explanation: There are 36 equally likely pairs, and 6 of them add to 7 (1 and 6, 2 and 5, 3 and 4, and the same pairs reversed). 6/36 = 1/6.

questions.stem: What is 2.4 ÷ 0.06?
questions.explanation: Multiply both numbers by 100 to get 240 ÷ 6 = 40. As a check, 40 × 0.06 = 2.4.

questions.stem: y is proportional to x, and y = 12 when x = 4. What is y when x = 10?
questions.explanation: y is always 3 times x because 12 ÷ 4 = 3, so y = 3 × 10 = 30. Adding 6 to both numbers gives 18, which is not proportional.

questions.stem: Using 3.14 for π, what is the area of a circle with a radius of 5 cm?
questions.explanation: Area is πr², so 3.14 × 5 × 5 = 78.5 square centimeters. 31.4 is the circumference, 2πr.

questions.stem: A bag has 4 red and 6 blue marbles. Two marbles are drawn without putting the first back. What is the probability that both are red?
questions.explanation: The first is red with probability 4/10, and then 3 of the 9 left are red, so 4/10 × 3/9 = 12/90 = 2/15. 4/25 would be right only if the first marble went back.

questions.stem: METICULOUS:
questions.explanation: A meticulous worker pays close attention to every detail, so careful is closest. Careless and messy are opposites.

questions.stem: SERENE:
questions.explanation: A serene lake or face is peaceful and calm. Serene and serious begin alike but mean different things.

questions.stem: DILIGENT:
questions.explanation: A diligent student keeps working steadily and with effort. Lazy is the opposite, and a person can be intelligent without being diligent.

questions.stem: OBSOLETE:
questions.explanation: Something obsolete is no longer used because something newer replaced it, so outdated is closest. An obsolete machine may still work, so broken is not the meaning.

questions.stem: BENEVOLENT:
questions.explanation: Benevolent comes from Latin words for wishing well, and it means kind and generous. Cruel is the opposite.

questions.stem: HOSTILE:
questions.explanation: A hostile crowd is unfriendly or even aggressive. Hospitable and welcoming mean the opposite.

questions.stem: PERPLEXED:
questions.explanation: A perplexed person is puzzled and confused. Certain is the opposite.

questions.stem: VERSATILE:
questions.explanation: A versatile tool or athlete can do many different things, so adaptable is closest. Limited is the opposite.

questions.stem: TRANQUIL:
questions.explanation: A tranquil garden is quiet and peaceful. Restless is the opposite, and transparent and tropical only share the opening letters.

questions.stem: LUCID:
questions.explanation: A lucid explanation is easy to understand, so clear is closest. Puzzling is the opposite, and lucky only looks similar.

questions.stem:
The hikers were _____ after the long climb, so they rested before going on.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: They needed to rest after a long climb, so they were exhausted. Energetic people would not need to stop.

questions.stem:
The puppy's _____ behavior delighted the children as it chased its own tail around the yard.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: Chasing its own tail is playful behavior. A sleepy or fearful puppy would not do this.

questions.stem:
Even though the test was difficult, Priya felt _____ because she had studied for weeks.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: Even though signals a contrast with difficult, and weeks of study explain why she felt confident. Anxious would match the difficulty, not contrast with it.

questions.stem:
Unlike her brother, who spends every penny, Lena is _____ and saves most of her allowance.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: Unlike signals a contrast with spending every penny, and saving most of her money shows she is economical. Wasteful describes her brother.

questions.stem:
Because the instructions were _____, half the class built the model incorrectly.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: Half the class made mistakes because of the instructions, so they must have been unclear. Helpful or accurate instructions would prevent mistakes.

questions.stem:
Omar remained _____ during the storm, calmly helping his younger cousins find flashlights.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: Calmly helping others shows he stayed composed. Frantic means wildly upset, the opposite of calm.

questions.stem:
The company decided to _____ the product after customers reported that it overheated.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: A product that overheats is unsafe, so the company would recall it, calling it back from buyers. Promoting or advertising it would sell more of a faulty product.

questions.stem:
The new law was _____: many people supported it, but just as many opposed it.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: A law that splits people into supporters and opponents is controversial. Popular would mean most people liked it.

questions.stem:
The author's _____ descriptions made readers feel as if they were standing in the market themselves.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: Descriptions that make readers feel they are really there are vivid, full of clear detail. Dull and vague descriptions would not do that.

questions.stem:
The ancient map was so _____ that the archivist handled it with gloves and great care.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: Old paper that must be handled with great care is brittle, easily cracked. Sturdy is the opposite, and the map is ancient, not modern.

questions.stem: Which number is both a multiple of 3 and a factor of 36?
questions.explanation: 12 = 3 × 4, and 36 ÷ 12 = 3, so it is both. 24 is a multiple of 3 but does not divide 36, and 15 does not divide 36.

questions.stem: Sam reads 15 pages in 20 minutes. At that rate, how many pages can he read in 1 hour?
questions.explanation: One hour is three 20-minute blocks, so he reads 3 × 15 = 45 pages.

questions.stem: Two angles of a triangle measure 40° and 75°. What is the measure of the third angle?
questions.explanation: The angles of a triangle add to 180°, and 180 - 40 - 75 = 65. The value 115° is just 40 + 75.

questions.stem: The value of x is 3 more than y, and y = 5. What is the value of 2x?
questions.explanation: x = 5 + 3 = 8, so 2x = 16. The value 8 is x itself, not 2x.

questions.stem: On a map, 1 inch stands for 20 miles. Two towns are 3.5 inches apart on the map. How far apart are they?
questions.explanation: Each inch is 20 miles, so 3.5 inches is 3.5 × 20 = 70 miles.

questions.stem: Which expression is equal to 6(x + 2)?
questions.explanation: Multiply both terms inside the parentheses by 6: 6 × x + 6 × 2 = 6x + 12. Writing 6x + 2 forgets to multiply the 2.

questions.stem: A bag holds 5 red, 3 green and 2 yellow cubes. One cube is picked at random. What is the probability that it is not red?
questions.explanation: 5 of the 10 cubes are not red (3 green and 2 yellow), and 5/10 = 1/2.

questions.stem: A square has an area of 49 square inches. What is its perimeter?
questions.explanation: The side is 7 inches because 7 × 7 = 49, so the perimeter is 4 × 7 = 28 inches. 196 comes from multiplying the area by 4.

questions.stem: The temperature rose from -4°F to 9°F. By how many degrees did it rise?
questions.explanation: From -4 up to 0 is 4 degrees, and from 0 up to 9 is 9 more, so it rose 13 degrees. Subtracting 4 from 9 gives 5, which ignores the sign.

questions.stem: Which number is the greatest?
questions.explanation: As decimals, 5/8 = 0.625, 61% = 0.61, and 0.6 and 3/5 are both 0.6, so 5/8 is the greatest.

questions.stem:
**Column A:** 0.05

**Column B:** 1/20

Which statement is true?
options: The quantity in Column A is greater.
The quantity in Column B is greater.
The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: 1/20 = 5/100 = 0.05, so the quantities are equal.

questions.stem:
**Column A:** The number of edges of a cube

**Column B:** The number of faces of a cube

Which statement is true?
options: The quantity in Column A is greater.
The quantity in Column B is greater.
The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: A cube has 12 edges and 6 faces, so Column A is greater.

questions.stem:
**Column A:** 3/5 of 40

**Column B:** 2/3 of 33

Which statement is true?
options: The quantity in Column A is greater.
The quantity in Column B is greater.
The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: 3/5 of 40 is 24 and 2/3 of 33 is 22, so Column A is greater.

questions.stem:
**Column A:** 7 × 98

**Column B:** 700 - 7

Which statement is true?
options: The quantity in Column A is greater.
The quantity in Column B is greater.
The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: 7 × 98 = 7 × 100 - 7 × 2 = 700 - 14 = 686, while 700 - 7 = 693. Column B is greater, and no long multiplication is needed.

questions.stem:
y < 0

**Column A:** y

**Column B:** -y

Which statement is true?
options: The quantity in Column A is greater.
The quantity in Column B is greater.
The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: If y is negative, then -y is positive, and any positive number is greater than a negative one.

questions.stem:
**Column A:** The probability of rolling an even number on a fair six-sided number cube

**Column B:** The probability that a fair coin lands heads

Which statement is true?
options: The quantity in Column A is greater.
The quantity in Column B is greater.
The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Three of the six faces are even, so the first probability is 3/6 = 1/2. A coin lands heads with probability 1/2 as well.

questions.stem:
n is a prime number.

**Column A:** n

**Column B:** 2

Which statement is true?
options: The quantity in Column A is greater.
The quantity in Column B is greater.
The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: The smallest prime is 2, so n could equal 2, but n could also be 3, 5 or any larger prime. It cannot be determined.

questions.stem:
The angles of a triangle measure x°, 2x° and 3x°.

**Column A:** x

**Column B:** 25

Which statement is true?
options: The quantity in Column A is greater.
The quantity in Column B is greater.
The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: The angles add to 180°, so x + 2x + 3x = 6x = 180 and x = 30, which is greater than 25.

questions.stem:
0 < m < 1

**Column A:** m²

**Column B:** m

Which statement is true?
options: The quantity in Column A is greater.
The quantity in Column B is greater.
The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Squaring a number between 0 and 1 makes it smaller: for example, (1/2)² = 1/4. So Column B is greater for every such m.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Trees paint their leaves to attract animals.
Fall colors come from pigments, some hidden all summer.
Carrots and corn get their bright color from chlorophyll.
Leaves turn red only after a hard freeze.
questions.explanation: The passage explains that yellows and oranges were there all summer and reds come from pigments made in fall. It says carotenoids color carrots, not chlorophyll.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why does a leaf keep making chlorophyll all summer?
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says chlorophyll breaks down in sunlight, so the leaf must keep replacing it.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, an autumn with cloudy days and warm nights would most likely produce:
questions.explanation: Sunny days followed by cool nights produce the brightest reds, so the opposite weather would likely mean duller reds.

questions.stem: As used in the last paragraph, the word "blaze" most nearly means:
questions.explanation: A forest that can blaze with color is shining with bright color. Nothing is actually burning, so burn down is too literal.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the second paragraph?
options: To describe the brightest fall forests on Earth
To compare maples with other trees
To explain why trees drop their leaves
To explain the pigments in a summer leaf
questions.explanation: The second paragraph names chlorophyll and carotenoids and explains why the green hides the yellow in summer.

questions.stem: The author's tone is best described as:
questions.explanation: The author calmly explains a scientific process with facts and examples.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: A fast mail service and why it ended
The life of one famous rider
Why California joined the United States
questions.explanation: The passage explains how the Pony Express worked and why the telegraph made it unnecessary. No single rider is named.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why were Pony Express riders young and light?
options: The saddles were made very small
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says the riders were light because every extra pound slowed a horse.

questions.stem: Which statement would the author most likely agree with?
options: The riders failed because they were careless.
New inventions can quickly replace old ways.
Ships carried mail faster than horses did.
The telegraph took years to replace the riders.
questions.explanation: The Pony Express shut down within days of the telegraph line, which shows an invention replacing an older method fast. The passage says ships took weeks.

questions.stem: As used in the first paragraph, the word "launched" most nearly means:
questions.explanation: To launch an experiment is to start it. Threw and sailed are other meanings of launch that do not fit an experiment.

questions.stem: How does the author organize the passage?
options: From the West Coast to the East
In time order, from start to end
As a set of letters from riders
questions.explanation: The passage moves from the problem in 1860, to how the service worked, to its end in 1861.

questions.stem: The phrase "lost its race" in the last sentence is an example of:
questions.explanation: The Pony Express did not run in a real race; the phrase compares the competition with the telegraph to a race.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the author's main point?
options: Libraries should stop buying new books.
Makerspaces belong in schools, not libraries.
A makerspace fits a library's true purpose.
questions.explanation: The author argues that libraries exist to share costly tools for learning, and a makerspace does exactly that.

questions.stem: Which detail does the author use to show that the makerspace leads people to books?
options: The room was once for storage
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says many makerspace visitors leave with a book under their arm.

questions.stem: The author mentions that books were once expensive in order to suggest that:
options: libraries have always shared costly tools
books are no longer worth reading
families today own too many books
makerspaces should charge every user a fee
questions.explanation: The comparison shows that lending a 3D printer today is like lending books in the past: both give everyone tools they could not easily own.

questions.stem: As used in the second paragraph, the word "access" most nearly means:
questions.explanation: Giving everyone access to tools means giving them the chance to use the tools.

questions.stem: How does the author respond to the people who were upset?
options: Explains their view, then disputes it
Quotes their angry letters at great length
questions.explanation: The author says, "I understand the worry," and then explains why it misses what libraries are for.

questions.stem: The author's tone is best described as:
questions.explanation: The author takes a clear side and supports it with reasons and examples, while still treating the critics politely.

questions.stem: What is 2/5 written as a percent?
If x/4 - 3 = 2, what is the value of x?
questions.explanation: Add 3 to get x/4 = 5, then multiply by 4: x = 20. Stopping at 5 forgets that x is divided by 4.

questions.stem: How many grams are in 2.5 kilograms?
questions.explanation: A kilogram is 1,000 grams, so 2.5 × 1,000 = 2,500 grams.

questions.stem: In a survey of 200 students, 35% said they walk to school. How many students walk?
questions.explanation: 35% of 200 is 0.35 × 200 = 70. 35 is the percent, not the number of students.

questions.stem: What is 1.2 × 0.3?
questions.explanation: 12 × 3 = 36, and the factors have two decimal places in all, so the product is 0.36. Adding the numbers gives 1.5 instead.

questions.stem: Each term in a pattern is 3 times the term before it, minus 1. The first term is 2. What is the fourth term?
questions.explanation: The terms are 2, then 3 × 2 - 1 = 5, then 3 × 5 - 1 = 14, then 3 × 14 - 1 = 41. 14 is the third term.

questions.stem: Three angles of a quadrilateral measure 90°, 85° and 100°. What is the measure of the fourth angle?
questions.explanation: The angles of a quadrilateral add to 360°, and 360 - 90 - 85 - 100 = 85. Using 180° as the total would give a negative answer, so it cannot be right.

questions.stem: A table shows the books checked out of a library: Monday 14, Tuesday 9, Wednesday 16 and Thursday 11. How many more books were checked out on the busiest day than on the slowest day?
questions.explanation: The busiest day, Wednesday, had 16 and the slowest, Tuesday, had 9: 16 - 9 = 7. 50 is the total for all four days.

questions.stem: What is 5/6 - 1/4?
questions.explanation: With a common denominator of 12, 10/12 - 3/12 = 7/12. Subtracting tops and bottoms separately gives 4/2 = 2, which is the common mistake.

questions.stem: What is the slope of the line through the points (1, 2) and (3, 8)?
questions.explanation: Slope is the change in y over the change in x: (8 - 2) ÷ (3 - 1) = 6 ÷ 2 = 3. Flipping the fraction gives 1/3.

questions.stem: Using 3.14 for π, what is the circumference of a circle with a diameter of 10 inches?
questions.explanation: Circumference is π × diameter, so 3.14 × 10 = 31.4 inches. 62.8 uses the diameter where the radius belongs in 2πr.

questions.stem: What is the median of 5, 12, 3, 9, 6 and 10?
questions.explanation: In order: 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 12. With an even count, the median is the mean of the middle two: (6 + 9) ÷ 2 = 7.5.
A negative times a negative is positive, so (-6) × (-4) = 24, and 24 ÷ 3 = 8.

questions.stem: Which expression is equivalent to 3(x + 4) - 2(x - 1)?
questions.explanation: 3(x + 4) = 3x + 12 and -2(x - 1) = -2x + 2, so the total is x + 14. Getting x + 10 multiplies the -1 by -2 incorrectly, as if it gave -2.

questions.stem: A trapezoid has parallel sides of 6 m and 10 m and a height of 4 m. What is its area?
questions.explanation: Area = half the sum of the parallel sides × height = (6 + 10) ÷ 2 × 4 = 8 × 4 = 32 square meters. Forgetting to halve gives 64.

questions.stem: A jar holds 30 marbles. The probability of picking a green marble is 2/5. How many marbles are green?
questions.explanation: 2/5 of 30 is 30 ÷ 5 × 2 = 12. 18 is the number that are not green.

questions.stem: The ratio of boys to girls in a class is 4 to 5. There are 36 students. How many are girls?
questions.explanation: Each group of 4 boys and 5 girls has 9 students, and 36 ÷ 9 = 4 groups, so there are 4 × 5 = 20 girls. 16 is the number of boys.

questions.stem: If n² = 64 and n < 0, what is n?
questions.explanation: Both 8 and -8 square to 64, and n must be negative, so n = -8. Dividing 64 by 2 gives 32, which is not a square root.

questions.stem: The point (3, -2) is reflected over the x-axis. Where does it land?
questions.explanation: Reflecting over the x-axis keeps x the same and changes the sign of y, so (3, -2) becomes (3, 2). (-3, -2) is the reflection over the y-axis.

questions.stem: A fair coin is flipped and a fair number cube numbered 1 to 6 is rolled. What is the probability of heads and a 6?
questions.explanation: The two events are independent, so multiply: 1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12. Adding them gives 2/3, which is not how "and" works.

questions.stem: Which number is the greatest?
questions.explanation: As decimals the numbers are -0.5, -0.45, -0.4 and about -0.33. The one closest to zero, -1/3, is the greatest.

questions.stem: A table shows x = 1, 2, 3, 4 paired with y = 5, 8, 11, 14. Which equation fits every pair?
questions.explanation: y goes up 3 each time x goes up 1, so y = 3x + b, and 5 = 3 × 1 + b gives b = 2. Check: 3 × 4 + 2 = 14. y = x + 4 fits only the first pair.

questions.stem: What is the surface area of a cube with edges 4 inches long?
questions.explanation: A cube has 6 square faces of 4 × 4 = 16 square inches each, so 6 × 16 = 96 square inches. 64 is the volume, in cubic inches.

questions.stem: Lena's first three test scores are 80, 85 and 90. What must she score on the fourth test for a mean of 87?
questions.explanation: A mean of 87 over 4 tests needs a total of 348. Her first three add to 255, so she needs 348 - 255 = 93.

questions.stem: RIGID:
questions.explanation: A rigid ruler does not bend, so stiff is closest. Bendable is the opposite.

questions.stem: MEAGER:
questions.explanation: A meager meal is small and not enough, so small is closest. Generous is the opposite, and eager only sounds similar.

questions.stem: GENUINE:
questions.explanation: A genuine diamond is real, or authentic. Fake is the opposite, and generous and gentle only look similar.

questions.stem: ADEQUATE:
questions.explanation: Adequate means good enough for what is needed, so sufficient is closest. Adequate is less than excellent, and lacking is the opposite.

questions.stem: FEROCIOUS:
questions.explanation: A ferocious animal is savage and fierce. Gentle is the opposite.

questions.stem: IMMENSE:
questions.explanation: Immense means extremely large, so huge is closest. Tiny is the opposite, and immediate only begins the same way.

questions.stem: PRUDENT:
questions.explanation: A prudent choice shows good judgment and care, so wise is closest. Reckless is the opposite.

questions.stem: LUMINOUS:
questions.explanation: A luminous object gives off light, so glowing is closest. Dim is the opposite, and enormous only shares the ending.

questions.stem: ABRUPT:
questions.explanation: An abrupt stop happens all at once, so sudden is closest. Gradual is the opposite.

questions.stem: COMPEL:
questions.explanation: To compel someone is to force them to act. Allow means to let someone choose, which is close to the opposite.

questions.stem:
The cafeteria was _____ at noon, with every table full and a line out the door.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: Every table full and a line out the door describe a packed room. Empty is the opposite.

questions.stem:
Despite his _____ start in the race, Leo caught up and finished second.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: Despite signals a contrast: he had to catch up, so his start was slow. A quick or strong start would leave nothing to catch up.

questions.stem:
The library's rules _____ eating near the computers, so Ana finished her snack outside.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: Ana went outside to eat, so the rules must forbid eating there. If the rules allowed it, she could have stayed.

questions.stem:
The river's current was too _____ for swimming, so the lifeguard raised a red flag.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: A red flag warns of danger, and a strong current is dangerous to swimmers. A gentle current would be safe.

questions.stem:
Lucia's _____ attitude made her a great team captain; she always expected the best.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: Always expecting the best is what optimistic means. Gloomy is the opposite.

questions.stem:
The scientist's notes were so _____ that another researcher could repeat every step exactly.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: Notes good enough to repeat every step must be thorough, complete in every detail. Sloppy or vague notes would leave steps out.

questions.stem:
The neighbors did the work without pay because they wanted to; their help was entirely _____.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: Working without pay because you want to is voluntary, given by choice. Required would mean they had no choice.

questions.stem:
Ravi's answer was _____; it had nothing to do with the question the teacher asked.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: An answer that has nothing to do with the question is irrelevant. It could still be detailed, but that is not what the second half explains.

questions.stem:
The team's victory was _____, since they had not won a single game all season.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: A team that had not won all season would not be expected to win, so the victory was unexpected. Predictable and routine are the opposite.

questions.stem:
Because the movie's ending was _____, viewers argued for days about what had really happened.

Which word best completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: Viewers argued about what happened, so the ending was mysterious, open to different readings. An obvious ending would leave nothing to argue about.

questions.stem: What is the least common multiple of 6 and 8?
questions.explanation: The multiples of 8 are 8, 16, 24, and 24 is the first that 6 also divides. 48, 72 and 96 are common multiples too, but not the least.

questions.stem: A cube has edges 3 cm long. What is its volume?
questions.explanation: Volume is length × width × height, so 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 cubic centimeters. 9 is the area of one face only.

questions.stem: If a > b and b > c, which statement must be true?
questions.explanation: a is greater than b, and b is greater than c, so a is greater than c.

questions.stem: A recipe uses 2 cups of flour for 12 cookies. How many cups are needed for 30 cookies?
questions.explanation: 30 cookies is 2.5 times 12, so the flour is 2.5 × 2 = 5 cups.

questions.stem: Three notebooks cost \$4.50. At the same price each, what do 7 notebooks cost?
The distance from 0 to 1 on a number line is split into 8 equal parts. A point sits on the third mark to the right of 0. What number does it show?
questions.explanation: Each part is 1/8, and three parts make 3/8. The fraction 5/8 counts the parts left between the point and 1.

questions.stem: A fair coin is flipped twice. What is the probability of getting heads both times?
questions.explanation: The four equally likely results are HH, HT, TH and TT, and only one is two heads. Treating HT and TH as one result gives 1/3, which is wrong because they are separate outcomes.

questions.stem: What is the median of 4, 9, 2, 7 and 5?
questions.explanation: In order the numbers are 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, and the middle one is 5. The mean, 5.4, is a different measure.

questions.stem: A town has 19,870 people. What is this number rounded to the nearest thousand?
questions.explanation: The hundreds digit is 8, which is 5 or more, so 19,870 rounds up to 20,000. 19,900 is the nearest hundred.

questions.stem: Jo is 4 years older than Max. In 5 years, the sum of their ages will be 32. How old is Max now?
questions.explanation: In 5 years Max will be m + 5 and Jo m + 9, so 2m + 14 = 32 and m = 9. Jo is 13 now, the age of the wrong person.

questions.stem:
**Column A:** 20% of 45

**Column B:** 1/4 of 36

Which statement is true?
options: The quantity in Column A is greater.
The quantity in Column B is greater.
The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: 20% of 45 is 45 ÷ 5 = 9, and 1/4 of 36 is 36 ÷ 4 = 9, so the quantities are equal.

questions.stem:
**Column A:** The number of minutes in 2 hours

**Column B:** The number of seconds in 2 minutes

Which statement is true?
options: The quantity in Column A is greater.
The quantity in Column B is greater.
The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: 2 hours is 120 minutes and 2 minutes is 120 seconds, so they are equal.

questions.stem:
**Column A:** -5 + 8

**Column B:** -8 + 5

Which statement is true?
options: The quantity in Column A is greater.
The quantity in Column B is greater.
The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: -5 + 8 = 3 and -8 + 5 = -3, so Column A is greater.

questions.stem:
**Column A:** √49

**Column B:** 2³ - 2

Which statement is true?
options: The quantity in Column A is greater.
The quantity in Column B is greater.
The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: √49 = 7 and 2³ - 2 = 8 - 2 = 6, so Column A is greater.

questions.stem:
p > q

**Column A:** p - q

**Column B:** 0

Which statement is true?
options: The quantity in Column A is greater.
The quantity in Column B is greater.
The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: If p is greater than q, then p - q is a positive number, which is greater than 0.

questions.stem:
**Column A:** The least prime number greater than 20

**Column B:** The greatest prime number less than 30

Which statement is true?
options: The quantity in Column A is greater.
The quantity in Column B is greater.
The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: The least prime above 20 is 23 (21 and 22 are not prime) and the greatest below 30 is 29, so Column B is greater.

**Column A:** 1/2 × 1/3

**Column B:** 1/2 - 1/3

options: The quantity in Column A is greater.
The quantity in Column B is greater.
The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

options: The quantity in Column A is greater.

**Column B:** 18

Which statement is true?
options: The quantity in Column A is greater.

A rectangle has an area of 36 square units.

**Column A:** The perimeter of the rectangle

**Column B:** 24 units

Which statement is true?
options: The quantity in Column A is greater.

questions.explanation: A 6 by 6 square has an area of 36 and a perimeter of 24, so the two could be equal. A 9 by 4 rectangle also has an area of 36, but its perimeter is 26. Different rectangles give different results, so it cannot be determined.

questions.stem:
**Column A:** The average speed of a car that travels 150 miles in 3 hours

**Column B:** The average speed of a car that travels 120 miles in 2 hours

Which statement is true?
options: The quantity in Column A is greater.

questions.explanation: The first car averages 150 ÷ 3 = 50 miles per hour and the second 120 ÷ 2 = 60 miles per hour, so Column B is greater.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How honeycomb is built in a hive
How honeybees share where food is
The childhood of an Austrian scientist
questions.explanation: The passage explains the waggle dance and how it tells other bees the direction and distance of food.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what does the length of the waggle run show?
options: How far away the food is
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says the longer the waggle run lasts, the farther away the flowers are.

questions.stem: If a bee waggles straight down the comb, the food is most likely:
questions.explanation: Straight up means toward the sun, and the angle from straight up matches the angle from the sun, so straight down means the opposite direction.

questions.stem: As used in the fourth paragraph, the word "symbolic" most nearly means:
questions.explanation: A symbolic map uses signs, here movements, to stand for real directions and distances.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the first paragraph?
options: To pose the problem the dance solves
To describe the parts of a hive
To explain von Frisch's early experiments
To compare bees with other insects
questions.explanation: It asks how a bee can tell others where food is without speaking, and the rest of the passage answers that question.

questions.stem: How does the author most likely feel about the waggle dance?
options: doubtful that it is real at all
questions.explanation: The author calls it one of the best-studied examples of animal communication and describes it with clear interest. The doubt in the passage belongs to early scientists, not the author.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Clay is the best material for any film.
Stop-motion builds movement slowly, by hand.
Modern films no longer use real frames.
Most animators dislike how slow their work is.
questions.explanation: The passage explains how every motion in stop-motion is built one photograph at a time by people.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why do puppets have armatures inside them?
options: To make them look much older
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says the metal skeletons let puppets hold each pose without sagging under hot lights.

questions.stem: An animator holds each pose for two frames. How many poses does she need for 5 seconds of film?
questions.explanation: Holding each pose for two frames means twelve poses per second, and 5 × 12 = 60. The number 120 is the count of frames, not poses.

questions.stem: As used in the second paragraph, the word "nudges" most nearly means:
questions.explanation: The animator nudges an arm a fraction of an inch, which means moves it just a little.

questions.stem: Why does the author ask a question at the start of the final paragraph?
options: To show the author is unsure
To change the subject to film cameras
To bring in why artists choose it
questions.explanation: The question "Why would anyone choose such a slow art?" leads straight into the animators' answer about handmade imperfections.

questions.stem: The phrase "part of the magic" suggests that the author views stop-motion as:
options: too slow to be worth the effort
questions.explanation: The author says the small flaws remind viewers that real hands made the film, and calls that part of the magic, which is praise.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: A doubted canal that changed trade
The early life story of DeWitt Clinton
Why wagons beat boats on cost
questions.explanation: The passage follows the Erie Canal from a mocked plan to a success that reshaped the nation's trade.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what did the locks do?
questions.explanation: The second paragraph defines locks as chambers that raised and lowered boats where the land climbed or fell.

questions.stem: The critics most likely "fell silent" when the canal opened because:
options: they had moved away to Buffalo
questions.explanation: Right after that phrase the passage describes how the canal cut shipping costs, so the critics had been proved wrong.

questions.stem: As used in the first paragraph, the word "championed" most nearly means:
questions.explanation: To champion a plan is to speak and work for it. Won is the sports meaning of champion, which does not fit here.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the last paragraph?
options: To describe how the canal was dug
To sum up the canal's effects
questions.explanation: It names the towns and the busy port that grew from the canal and ends by saying it changed the nation's trade.

questions.stem: The quotation marks around "ditch" in the last paragraph suggest that the author:
questions.explanation: The critics had mocked the canal as Clinton's Ditch. Putting the word in quotation marks recalls that insult, now proved wrong.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the theme of the story?
options: Books make good gifts for pets.
Puppies are much easier to love than older dogs.
Trust grows through patience, not force.
questions.explanation: Biscuit comes to Tamsin only after she stops reaching for him and waits quietly.

questions.stem: What did Mr. Reyes tell Tamsin to do with Biscuit?
options: Feed him a treat very slowly
Walk him around the shelter yard
questions.explanation: Mr. Reyes says, "Don't reach for him. Just be there." Reading aloud was Tamsin's own idea.

questions.stem: Tamsin most likely avoids looking at Biscuit while she reads in order to:
questions.explanation: Biscuit is frightened of people, so not staring at him helps him feel safe enough to come closer.

questions.stem: As used in the fifth paragraph, the word "crept" most nearly means:
questions.explanation: Biscuit crept out, coming forward carefully and quietly. A frightened dog would not jump out quickly.

questions.stem: How does the first paragraph prepare for the rest of the story?
options: It gives Biscuit's whole history in detail.
It sets up a contrast with what happens.
It explains how shelters are run.
It describes Mr. Reyes at length.
questions.explanation: Tamsin imagines playful puppies and kittens, but her real afternoon brings cleaning and a frightened dog, a contrast the story builds on.

questions.stem: In the last sentence, "the answer" refers to:
questions.explanation: The chin on her knee is called almost like a question; the answer she hopes for is Biscuit trusting her, so she keeps still.

questions.stem: What is 3/8 of 64?
questions.explanation: 64 ÷ 8 = 8, and 3 × 8 = 24. The value 8 is only one eighth.

questions.stem: Which expression is equivalent to 7a + 3b - 2a + b?
questions.explanation: Combine the a terms, 7a - 2a = 5a, and the b terms, 3b + b = 4b. A lone b counts as 1b, so 5a + 3b drops it.

questions.stem: Two lines cross. One of the angles they form measures 72°. What is the angle directly across from it?
questions.explanation: Angles directly across from each other where two lines cross are vertical angles, and they are equal. 108° is the angle beside it, which is supplementary.

questions.stem: Ken has 3 shirts and 4 pairs of pants. How many different outfits of one shirt and one pair of pants can he make?
questions.explanation: Each of the 3 shirts goes with each of the 4 pairs of pants, so there are 3 × 4 = 12 outfits. 7 adds them instead.

questions.stem: What is |-7| + |3|?
questions.explanation: The absolute value of a number is its distance from 0, so |-7| = 7 and |3| = 3, and 7 + 3 = 10.

questions.stem: Which equation means "twice a number decreased by 7 is 19"?
questions.explanation: Twice a number is 2n, and decreased by 7 means subtract 7 from it: 2n - 7 = 19. 2(n - 7) would mean the number was decreased first, then doubled.

questions.stem: How many milliliters are in 1.5 liters?
questions.explanation: A liter is 1,000 milliliters, so 1.5 × 1,000 = 1,500.

questions.stem: The letters of the word MATH are written on cards and one card is picked at random. What is the probability of picking a vowel?
questions.explanation: Only A is a vowel, so the probability is 1 out of 4. 3/4 is the probability of a consonant.

questions.stem: Which improper fraction is equal to 3 2/5?
questions.explanation: 3 wholes are 15 fifths, and 15 + 2 = 17, so 3 2/5 = 17/5. Writing the digits side by side as 32/5 is a common slip.

questions.stem: If 5 - 2(x + 1) = -7, what is the value of x?
A triangle has a base of 10 cm and a height of 7 cm. What is its area?
questions.explanation: Area is half of base × height: 10 × 7 ÷ 2 = 35 square centimeters. 70 forgets to take half.

questions.stem: The data set 3, 6, 6, 8 and 11 has a mode of 6. Which number, added to the set, would give the set two modes?
questions.explanation: Adding 8 makes both 6 and 8 appear twice, so there are two modes. Adding 6 keeps a single mode, and 7 or 10 would appear only once.

questions.stem: The price of a game rose from \$40 to \$50. What was the percent increase?
questions.explanation: The increase is \$10, and \$10 out of the original \$40 is 1/4, or 25%. Dividing by the new price, \$50, gives 20% instead.

questions.stem: The sum of three consecutive integers is 48. What is the least of them?
questions.explanation: Call them n, n + 1 and n + 2: 3n + 3 = 48, so n = 15, and 15 + 16 + 17 = 48. 16 is the middle one.

questions.stem: A rectangle 8 m by 5 m is enlarged by a scale factor of 2. What is the area of the new rectangle?
questions.explanation: The new rectangle is 16 m by 10 m, so its area is 160 square meters, four times the old 40. Doubling the area to 80 forgets that both sides double.

questions.stem: The mean of six numbers is 9. One of the numbers, 14, is removed. What is the mean of the five numbers left?
questions.explanation: The six numbers add to 6 × 9 = 54. Removing 14 leaves 40, and 40 ÷ 5 = 8.
